Part 3:
BFS has a peak of 5, whereas DFS peaks at 10 with a deepest branch of 10. My algorithm's model matches neither, since mine utilises a heap whose per-entry cost grows as well as entry count. Empirically, peak_heap_pathlen, that describes the sum of all simultaneous entries (same as what O(VE) describes), grows at O(V^1.086). Since this is essentially linear O(V), it traces to 1 factor, the entry count stabilising at around 15, regardless of V (as if an asymptote exists). Since the paths dictionary is (as shown below) growing at a rate of V^0.738, doubling the approximated memory accounts for this O(kV) retained paths dictionary. So, as shown in the table above, a space class of O(V) at 200,000 node scale uses roughly 12.2 MB, and so doubling is 24.4 MB which obviously fits in the small drone.

The visited set is O(V). Frontier for Dijkstra's uses a heap that stores full copied paths per entry (path + [neighbour]) instead of parent pointers. So, it is O(V) per entry. Since O(E) entries are possible, frontier space is O(VE). The paths dictionary is O(kV) and is active after Dijkstra is completed. State_Space_Search's recursion stack is len(remaining) + len(order) which is always equal to k. Across k+1 depths, it is exactly k(k+1) = O(k^2), validated against 432,000 seeds.

Part 2:
Overall worst-case space is O(VE) + O(kV) + O(k^2), dominated by Dijkstra frontier (the other 2 are smaller in size comparatively). But
B&B is run after Dijkstra is freed..

Part 3:
BFS has a peak of 5, DFS peaks at 10 with a deepest branch of 10. My algorithm's model matches neither, since it utilises a heap whose per-entry cost grows as well as entry count. Across 432,000 seeds, peak_heap_pathlen, grew at O(V^1.086). Since it's almost linear O(V), it traces to entry count stabilising at 15-ish (as if asymptotic). Since this never approaches O(E), in the O(VE) bound, only V scales while entry count, O(E), doesn't. 

Part 4:
At V = 200,000, O(VE) gives roughly 2.3TB of memory which is completely infeasible. However, since data (below) has a power curve of V^1.086, extrapolation gives 34.9 MB. Since the paths dictionary grows at rate V^0.738, adding O(V) linear memory accounts for this ~ 12.2 MB, so total is 47.1 MB, which obviously fits. For recursion stack to be more costly, over 447 supplies need to exist (square-root of V, 200,000 in this case, stack gives O(V) memory), and even then, total memory needed is still 47.1 MB (as Dijkstra RAM is freed and available), and is fine.

Neither option fits. Shortest_Paths_Dict_Constructor attempts to find len(k) + len(exits) targets per call, so can't be Ω(1). However, early termination on discovery of all targets means it isn't Θ(V+E) either. Both stages (Dijkstra & Branch-&-Bound) are Ω(k^2). Dijkstra needs k+1 calls, each needing k pops at minimum, giving k^2. Branch and bound needs at minimum 1 full descent of k + 1 nodes. With every call O(k) work, total is k^2. 

However, these best costs can't be achieved together as pruning (in B&B) requires large cost differences between collection orders. However, clustering supplies and exits, which make Dijkstra cheap, causes low cost variances, and this massively reduces the effectiveness of pruning, causing branch-and-bound to do near-maximal work. This correlation was confirmed through data across 12 million seeds of varying facility sizes (graph above). Preprocessing and search operations correlate negatively (r=-0.28) at V = 200 (against 3.75 million seeds). 

Part 2 (Single target):
Best case is 1 operation. Exit A and B respectively are 74 and 81 expansions. However, this isn't applicable to my algorithm as mine solves multi-target min-cost supply collection ordering.

Part 3:
Mission planning shouldn't rely on best case bounds. In practical applications, supply/exit clustering isn't guaranteed, and so operation count is closer to worst case. Plus, using worst-case instead is a guarantee, cause the target is guaranteed to be somewhere in the facility.

The built in trial slider simulates single-target BFS. However, as I established in S2-A, it doesn't represent any component of my staged algorithm. Running it would give figures that aren't relevant. However, the seed sweep data collected earlier works here. Across V = 200 to 6000, the mean op_pre grew with a fitted exponent of 2.05, matching the V^2 term in theoretical worst-case bound O(kV^2). At V = 6000, the data gives an average op_pre of 30.59 million, against a theoretical worst-case of kV^2 = 180 million. The cause is that the bound assumes all heap entries are near V length, but most paths on such mazes are much shorter. The empirical mean is constantly 5.9 times smaller. Both stages confirm average case is Θ(kV^2), same as worst-case bound, but with a much smaller constant - 5.9x smaller. 

Part 3:
The average informs the typical cost for realistic responses, whereas worst-case informs maximal runtime in clustered supply layouts. Reporting the average alone causes underestimation of possible worst-case scenarios, but reporting only worst-case understates the effectiveness of the algorithm on all other cases.

I assumed instances of random, spanning tree like facilities, where supplies are uniformly and randomly placed. In these cases, the target is the combined set of supplies and exits. Another view is where supplies and exits are clustered. This though causes the average case to approach the worst case (since greater search and branch and bound operations must be conducted).

Part 2:
The built in tester is for single target BFS and doesn't fit my algorithm. However, the aggregated seed sweep data does apply here. Across sizes of V = 200 to 6000, the mean op_pre grew with an exponent of 2.05, equivalent to the V^2 term in the theoretical worst-case bound O(kV^2). At V = 6000, the data gave an average op_pre of 30.59 million operations, whereas theoretically, it is worst-case kV^2 = 180 million. This is caused by the fact that the bound assumed all Dijkstra heap entries are V-1 in length. However, realistically, the paths in these structures are way smaller. 

The mean op_pre is consistently 5.9 times smaller. This type of pattern can be seen in op_search, where it averages 1090, versus worst-case of 3000. Both confirm that average case is Θ(kV^2), the same as the worst-case, but with a much smaller constant.

Part 3:
The average informs the typical cost for realistic responses, whereas worst-case informs maximal runtime in clustered supply layouts. Reporting the average alone causes underestimation of possible worst-case scenarios, but reporting only worst-case understates the effectiveness of the algorithm on all other cases.
S2C_space:
Part 1: 
The visited set is O(V). Frontier for Dijkstra's uses a heap that stores full copied paths per entry (path + [neighbour]) instead of parent pointers. So, it is O(V) per entry. Since O(E) entries are possible, frontier space is O(VE). The paths dictionary is O(kV) and is active after Dijkstra is completed. State_Space_Search's recursion stack is len(remaining) + len(order) which is always equal to k. Across k+1 depths, it is exactly k(k+1) = O(k^2), validated against 432,000 seeds.

Part 2:
Overall worst-case space is O(VE) + O(kV) + O(k^2), dominated by Dijkstra frontier (the other 2 are smaller in size comparatively). But
B&B is run after Dijkstra is freed..

Part 3:
BFS has a peak of 5, DFS peaks at 10 with a deepest branch of 10. My algorithm's model matches neither, since it utilises a heap whose per-entry cost grows as well as entry count. Across 432,000 seeds, peak_heap_pathlen, grew at O(V^1.086). Since it's almost linear O(V), it traces to entry count stabilising at 15-ish (as if asymptotic). Since this never approaches O(E), in the O(VE) bound, only V scales while entry count, O(E), doesn't. 

Part 4:
At V = 200,000, O(VE) gives roughly 2.3TB of memory which is completely infeasible. However, since data (below) has a power curve of V^1.086, extrapolation gives 34.9 MB. Since the paths dictionary grows at rate V^0.738, adding O(V) linear memory accounts for this ~ 12.2 MB, so total is 47.1 MB, which obviously fits. For recursion stack to be more costly, over 447 supplies need to exist (square-root of V, 200,000 in this case, stack gives O(V) memory), and even then, total memory needed is still 47.1 MB (as Dijkstra RAM is freed and available), and is fine.

Neither option fits. Shortest_Paths_Dict_Constructor attempts to find len(k) + len(exits) targets per call, so can't be Ω(1). However, early termination on discovery of all targets means it isn't Θ(V+E) either. Both stages (Dijkstra & Branch-&-Bound) are Ω(k^2). Dijkstra needs k+1 calls, each needing k pops at minimum, giving k^2. Branch and bound needs at minimum 1 full descent of k + 1 nodes. With every call O(k) work, total is k^2. 

However, these best costs can't be achieved together as pruning (in B&B) requires large cost differences between collection orders. However, clustering supplies and exits, which make Dijkstra cheap, causes low cost variances, and this massively reduces the effectiveness of pruning, causing branch-and-bound to do near-maximal work. This correlation was confirmed through data across 12 million seeds of varying facility sizes (graph above). Preprocessing and search operations correlate negatively (r=-0.28) at V = 200 (against 3.75 million seeds). 

Part 2 (Single target):
Best case is 1 operation. Exit A and B respectively are 74 and 81 expansions. However, this isn't applicable to my algorithm as mine solves multi-target min-cost supply collection ordering.

Part 3:
Mission planning shouldn't rely on best case bounds. In practical applications, supply/exit clustering isn't guaranteed, and so operation count is closer to worst case. Plus, using worst-case instead is a guarantee, cause the target is guaranteed to be somewhere in the facility.

The visited set is O(V) memory. The frontier for Dijkstra uses a heap that stores full copied paths per entry (path + [neighbour]) instead of a parent pointer dictionary. So, it is O(V) per entry. Since O(E) entries are possible in worst-case, the frontier space is O(VE). The paths dictionary is O(k^2 * V) and is active after Dijkstra is completed. State_Space_Search's recursion stack is len(remaining) + len(order) which is always equal to k. Across k+1 depths, it is exactly k(k+1) = O(k^2), validated against 432,000 seeds.

Part 2:
Overall worst-case space is O(VE) + O(k^2 * V) + O(k^2), dominated by Dijkstra frontier (the other 2 are smaller in size comparatively). But B&B is run after Dijkstra is freed.

Part 3:
BFS has a peak of 5, DFS peaks at 10 with a deepest branch of 10. My algorithm's model matches neither, since it utilises a heap whose per-entry cost grows as well as entry count. Across 432,000 seeds, peak_heap_pathlen, grew at O(V^1.086). Since it's almost linear O(V), it traces to entry count stabilising at 15-ish (as if asymptotic). Since this never approaches O(E), in the O(VE) bound, only V scales while entry count, O(E), doesn't. 

Part 4:
At V = 200,000, O(VE) gives roughly 2.3TB of memory which is completely infeasible. However, since data (below) has a power curve of V^1.086, extrapolation gives 34.9 MB. Since the paths dictionary grows at rate V^0.738, adding O(V) linear memory accounts for this ~ 12.2 MB, so total is 47.1 MB, which obviously fits. For recursion stack to be more costly, over 447 supplies need to exist (square-root of V, 200,000 in this case, stack gives O(V) memory), and even then, total memory needed is still 47.1 MB (as Dijkstra RAM is freed and available), and is fine.
